title: Al-Bukhari's journey
hookLine: al-Bukhari travels for years, sifting hundreds of thousands of reports to compile his Sahih

lines: A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH INTENTION.
A MAN WITH A HARD QUESTION.
cards: A great book of reports about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, could have opened with a miracle, a battle or a law. This one opens with a sentence about the inside of a person.
The Prophet says that actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. That's the first report in the Sahih of al-Bukhari.
Before a single rule about prayer or trade, the reader is asked: why are you doing this? Fitting, because the man who built it spent his life on a hard question of his own.

teach.b: His name was Muhammad ibn Isma'il, called al-Bukhari after Bukhara, the city he came from. His question was simple to say and hard to answer: did the Prophet really say this?
A hadith is a report, and each one comes with a chain of people: I heard it from her, who heard it from him, who heard it from a companion of the Prophet.

teach.h: TEST EVERY LINK IN THE CHAIN.
teach.b: Al-Bukhari traveled from city to city to meet the people who carried those chains, and he tested every link. Did these two people actually meet? Was each one honest?
Was each one careful, with a strong memory? One weak link, and the report didn't go into his book, however lovely its words.

teach.h: IF AN EVIL-LIVER BRING YOU TIDINGS, VERIFY.
teach.b: The Qur'an gives the instinct behind it, in Pickthall's translation: "If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it."
Tradition says he heard a vast number of reports and kept only a small share, and that before writing each one down he would wash and pray.
The result is the Sahih, which means sound.
For Sunni Muslims it holds a place of deep trust, often named together with the collection of his student, Muslim.
Shia Muslims also hold the Prophet's words in deep trust, and gather and weigh reports through their own collections and scholars, especially those passed down through the Prophet's family.
Both care about the same thing: that what's said in the Prophet's name is really his.

how: Sunni Muslims read and teach Sahih al-Bukhari as a trusted collection of the Prophet's sayings, and students still learn to examine a report's chain of narrators; Shia Muslims rely on their own hadith collections and methods.

o: a pilgrimage he made on foot from Bukhara to Mecca
the long road he took to sell his books in Baghdad
his travels to test each chain of hadith, link by link

s: a report was judged only by whether its words sounded wise
al-Bukhari tested the chain: did the narrators meet, were they honest, were they careful.
al-Bukhari's Sahih opens with a report about intentions
its first report: actions are judged by intentions.
Sunni and Shia Muslims rely on the same hadith collections
Shia Muslims have their own collections and methods, with reports passed down through the Prophet's family.

games.q: a story people tell: you've traveled a long way to hear a report from a man. you find him calling his animal with a bag held out as if it had food in it, but the bag is empty. what do you do?
o: take down his report; it's a long way home.
turn around without taking the report.
ask a friend whether the report sounds right.
games.why: in the story, al-Bukhari turns back: a man who would deceive an animal might not be careful with words about the Prophet. it's told as a story about how seriously he took each link.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you heard or read this week and simply believed, a headline, a health tip, something a friend said, and trace the chain the way al-Bukhari would: who told you, where did they get it, did they see it or only hear it?
You don't have to decide it's false; just notice where your knowing stops. If you pray, you can ask for help to speak only what's true; if not, just hold the question: how do I know?

wordCard.voice: Al-Bukhari's journey. The scholar from Bukhara who traveled to test every chain of reports and gathered the ones he judged sound. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: sound, authentic; the name given to al-Bukhari's collection.

carryVoice: Your line: sifted with care. One weak link, and the report stayed out. Day nine hundred thirty, done.
